newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: S.E. Asian currencies plumb new depths.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asian currencies plumb new depths.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies plumbed new depths on Thursday and could fall further as speculative attacks give way to hedging, analysts said.
The Thai baht, which led the decline, recovered from lows of around 32.70 to the dollar, but continued to look vulnerable against a backdrop of bad financial sector news.
The relatively resilient Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure, falling through the psychological 1.47 level against the U.S. dollar on stop-loss sales.
And the Malaysian ringgit crashed to an early low of 2.6540 to the dollar on spillover weakness and continued to look depressed.

"It's a brave man who speculates in these markets now," said Tim Lucas, treasury manager at Bank of Bermuda in Hong Kong. "What's happening now is genuine portfolio hedging and genuine concern as opposed to having a speculative play."
The baht suffered again after only seven of 18 finance and securities firms reporting half year results made a profit. The sector's losses totalled a depressing 3.5 billion baht (US$108 million).

There was talk the central Bank of Thailand (BOT) had intervened to sell dollars above the 32.60 baht level, helping the baht stage a mild recovery. A BOT official declined to confirm or deny the market talk.
The baht was at 31.950/32.020 to the dollar onshore at 0955 GMT and 31.930/32.030 offshore.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said he would announce a major economic package within two weeks that would help stabilise the baht and bring down Thai interest rates.

Dealers attributed the Singapore dollar's sharp drop to Finance Minister Richard Hu's comments about Singapore's competitiveness not being hurt by the recent tumble of other Southeast Asian currencies.
Hu told parliament on Wednesday Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand and it would continue to be managed on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective.
The Singapore dollar fell to a 32-month low of 1.4785 and was quoted at 1.4770/75 at 1000 GMT.
"It was mainly interbank stop-losses being triggered and we've broken out of all the highs for the last few years," said the regional currency chief at a European bank.
The U.S. dollar could reach S$1.50 within a month if regional turmoil persisted, he said.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's call for cooperation among Southeast Asian countries to fight currency speculators gave the ringgit market brief pause, dealers said.
But the ringgit soon succumbed to selling again as players shrugged the comments off as just a suggestion.
The Indonesian rupiah was back below the 2,600 level to the dollar in late trade but its decline was relatively muted, partly due to signs the central bank had been intervened.
"The rupiah is moving in a steady mode compared to the rest. So they're not that alarmed. I think they're just trying to smooth the flow," one dealer said.
The rupiah was at 2,613/23 against an opening at 2,575/85.
The Philippine peso ended steady at 28.500/550 to the dollar against its previous 28.5.
Hong Kong dollar forwards remained near their highs despite talk of heavy intervention by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
Dealers said funds were buying the U.S. dollar forward, anticipating a fall in the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged at HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.
